summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; the operative instrument since 2010 is an anti-discrimination law that covers sexual orientation but provides no basis for same-sex marriage. A National LGBTI Action Plan runs from 2021 to 2027, and observers record that implementation falls short of its commitments.

Nothing in the record indicates trans-specific screening at the border or on arrival, and no restriction on facilities or bathrooms is on record. Police targeting of trans visitors is not documented in any source here. The realistic exposure is social rather than legal: Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people in 2023, and hostility is sharper outside Tirana and in more conservative rural areas. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

International scrutiny is unusually open for the region. Graeme Reid, the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, carried out a country visit from 1 to 12 July 2024, issued an end-of-mission statement on 12 July 2024, and presented report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 on 17 June 2025 assessing Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards. EU candidate status is the stated driver of slow alignment with those standards.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. An Anti-Discrimination Commissioner receives and mediates complaints, and has ruled against public figures who made hostile statements about LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
Parliamentary rhetoric has at times been openly hostile to LGBT work. In July 2021 Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a suspicious, revolting agenda, and MP Nard Ndoka used Facebook to brand the government LGBT and accuse it of pushing LGBT values in schools. Both episodes fall under the Berisha-led opposition and illustrate the political environment in which domestic advocacy operates.

The Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu in October 2011 after he told parliament that homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones, warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. Ten years later the same office mediated complaints about screenings of the film 'Strange World', ruling in favour of the complainant in one case.

Prime Minister Sali Berisha voiced support for same-sex marriage in July 2009, framing the anti-discrimination law as an EU-integration measure. That posture, combined with the 2024 UN country visit, marks Albania as more institutionally receptive than several neighbouring jurisdictions, though the gap between policy and practice remains the recurring finding of the international reviews.
localsOnly:
Residents seek redress through the 2010 anti-discrimination law and the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner's complaints process, which has produced both mediated settlements and rulings against prominent public figures.

Community organisations run material support schemes for the most exposed residents, including food packages distributed to trans sex workers and to people living with HIV. Rainbowphilia's casework recorded ten bias-motivated violence incidents against trans people in 2023.

The National LGBTI Action Plan 2021–2027 is the domestic policy framework covering education, health and non-discrimination work, but assessments of its delivery record gaps between the plan's targets and what has been implemented. Anti-LGBT messaging from elected officials has repeatedly surfaced around school-based education campaigns, shaping the environment for teachers and student groups.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced information on legal gender recognition in Albania, on rules for changing name or sex markers on identity documents, or on whether such changes affect passport presentation at entry. This is unresolved here, not established either way.

No source addresses visa or border screening procedures that could disclose a visitor's trans status, nor any restriction or requirement affecting access to hormone therapy or other trans-specific healthcare while in the country.

Sentencing outcomes and enforcement results for the ten bias-motivated violence cases logged in 2023 are not stated, so the effectiveness of criminal-law responses to that violence cannot be assessed from these sources.

The two Koha Jonё items carry 2018 URLs but 2021 publication dates; the discrepancy is unresolved. Whether the implementation deficits identified in the National LGBTI Action Plan have been remedied following the July 2024 visit and the June 2025 report is likewise not sourced.
